issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is poorly matched to the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. 'People in uniform' more strongly suggests assault/police/military trauma than a pediatric medical crisis, and there are no accompanying medical or hospital-related cues to make this clinically coherent.

This creates a hard-to-explain mismatch with the trauma context and with the trigger items, which are hospital/illness-related.

vignette:
Boonsong Rattanaporn is a 47-year-old Thai American man who has worked as a park ranger in the Pacific Northwest for nearly two decades. He is married, the father of two children, and by most external measures a steady and capable man - someone colleagues describe as calm in a crisis, reliable on the trail. He came to the intake appointment looking tired in a way that sleep does not seem to fix, and within the first session it became clear that he has been carrying something for several years that has grown heavier rather than lighter with time.

Three years ago, Boonsong's younger son, then nine years old, collapsed during a school soccer game. What followed was eleven days in the pediatric intensive care unit - a bacterial infection that had moved to the boy's heart, a series of interventions that the attending physicians described as touch-and-go. Boonsong spent most of those eleven days in the hospital, sleeping in a chair beside his son's bed, watching nurses move in and out of the room with an efficiency that he found both reassuring and terrifying. The ward had a particular smell - antiseptic, faintly chemical, undercut by something he could not name - and the nurses cleaned surfaces and IV lines with alcohol swabs so frequently that the odor became inseparable from the sound of monitors and the sight of his son's pale face against the pillow. On the third day, his son lost consciousness briefly during a procedure, and Boonsong himself became lightheaded and had to be helped to a chair in the corridor, his vision narrowing at the edges, the floor seeming to tilt beneath him. His son survived and has since recovered fully. Boonsong has not.

In the months that followed, he found himself consumed by a particular kind of anger that he has struggled to articulate clearly. The infection had been misdiagnosed twice at an urgent care clinic before the hospital admission, and Boonsong has come to believe that those delays nearly killed his child. He ruminates extensively about this - not in a way that moves toward resolution, but in a way that circles and tightens. He rehearses what he should have said to the urgent care physicians, imagines confrontations, constructs arguments. He dwells on what was done to his family, returning again and again to a sense of injury that feels fresh each time he revisits it. This rumination occupies him during long stretches of his working day, when he is alone on trail patrols through quiet forest, and it is precisely during these extended cycles of dwelling and rehearsing grievance that the sensory world seems to reach back at him. The smell of alcohol-based hand sanitizer - present at ranger stations, at trailhead facilities, carried by hikers - cuts through his concentration and pulls him back to the PICU ward with a vividness that is disorienting. The sharp antiseptic smell of cleaning products used in park restrooms has the same effect. And when the rumination is most intense, when he has spent an hour mentally relitigating the urgent care visits, he notices the dizziness returning - the same narrowing sensation he experienced in that hospital corridor - arriving not in response to any external threat but apparently from within, as though his body is following the mind's itinerary back to the worst days of his life.

He has begun avoiding situations in which the event might be mentioned. When his wife tries to discuss what happened - sometimes in the context of their son's follow-up appointments, sometimes simply as part of processing a frightening shared memory - Boonsong withdraws or changes the subject. He has declined two family gatherings at which a relative who was present during the hospitalization would also be present. A colleague who lost a child to illness attempted to confide in him last spring, and Boonsong found a reason to end the conversation and has kept his distance since. The avoidance had drawn its own map around him: the ranger stations he rerouted through, the trailhead restrooms he now noticed and braced against, the hand sanitizer dispensers at park facilities that he had never registered before - all of it had become more visible, more charged, precisely because the shape of what he was avoiding had made the sensory world into a landscape of reminders. His strategies for keeping the event at bay had, in effect, kept him oriented toward it. These avoidances have cost him something; his wife has told him, carefully but plainly, that she feels alone in what they went through.

What finally brought him to seek help was a near-miss on the trail last month - a moment of dizziness while navigating a steep ridge that he recognized, afterward, as dangerous. He is most afraid that the anger is permanent. What he hopes, though he said it quietly and only once, is that he might be able to remember his son's recovery without feeling like he is still inside the crisis.
